The Organismal Biology and Ecology (OBE) Department studies the structure and function of organisms in an ecological and evolutionary context. OBE encompasses cross-disciplinary approaches such as physiological ecology, evolutionary ecology, systematics, and biogeography, which all provide complementary insights into the processes of evolutionary diversification and adaptation to life on earth. Our research foci include botany, animal and plant ecology, comparative physiology, conservation biology, and molecular ecology. We strive to perform cutting-edge research and include students in these opportunities.
The focused three and a half week course style of the block plan enables our OBE faculty to design field/lab classes and research opportunities that are not possible in traditional school settings.
Field courses: Our exceptional location is adjacent to rich and diverse ecosystems situated at the range limits of many species of plants and animals. In an east-west direction, the elevation changes from roughly 6,000 to over 14,000 feet on top of Pikes Peak, resulting in a mosaic of ecosystems spanning plains, forests and tundra. Many classes take day-long, overnight or multi-day trips to explore sites near and far. Some of these are camping trips, but we also utilize the CC Cabin in the montane pine forests of the Pikes Peak foothills an hour from campus as well as the CC Baca Campus in the San Luis Valley three hours to the southwest. We also offer regular block-long field courses to Belize and Patagonia!
Small Class Size: Colorado College limits class sizes to a maximum of 25 students; most field and lab courses have even smaller sizes. This allows each student to receive individual attention, and to do investigative projects even in their first biology class.

We encourage and financially support collaborative student-faculty research projects. These opportunities provide excellent experience for students interested in graduate school or those planning on becoming part of a research team upon graduation.

content:Speaker user says: I'm not sure if it is still the case, but there was a time when Kuhn's book was the most frequently cited book in scientific literature. With all respect to my fellow reviewers, it might be a tad bit arrogant to dismiss such a book as "puerile." Before Kuhn, we were taught in school that scientific progress was linear, that it was an unending progression of refinements and developments, with one "truth" leading to the next "truth." Kuhn's insights including pointing out that such a linear progression was mostly a lie. His thesis was that the major developments in science were mostly revolutionary. That some "truths" turned out to be False. Astronomy was revolutionized by Galileo and Copernicus, and man was divested from the center of the universe. Physics was revolutionized by Newton. Biology and Darwin. It didn't hurt that plate tectonics came along shortly after Kuhn published, and Kuhn looked like his model was predictive, too. Part of Kuhn's impact, I have to admit, was a result of the time which the book was first published. In the middle and late 1960s, questioning authority was the heart of any undergraduate's thinking, and Kuhn's ideas were read by some as a license to question all authority. Perhaps as a consequence, Kuhn's model has been carried by other writers beyond all reason, with everyone from sociologists to New Age fuzzies usurping his terminology, making "paradigm shift" a nearly instant cliche. But his influence has gone far beyond those who want to mis-apply his ideas to everything from post-modern dance to sociobiology. Uniformitarianism has been bloodied, perhaps permanently. By geologists, evolutionists, archaeologists and more; the influence has been pervasive and real. Stephen Jay Gould may or may not subscribe to "Structure," but he has sure demolished uniformitarianism in evolution. I disagree with those who regard "Structure" as "the most important" anything. But it unquestionably has been stunningly influential, and any serious student of science or philosophy, I believe, will be reading this book a hundred years from now. And apart from its influence and impact, the book still reads well almost 40 years on. It's fun and, if you enjoy seeing the world stood on its ear, you'll like Kuhn's approach. context:The Language of Life keywords: Kuhn, paradigm shift, scientific progress, scientific literature, revisionism, plate tectonics, uniformity, evolution, Stephen Jay Gould, structure tags: Structure, Revolutions, Science, Reading, Evolution, Stephen Jay Gould

content:Speaker assistant says: Games have the potential to enhance student learning of biological concepts in several ways. First, they can provide a more interactive and engaging learning environment than traditional forms of instruction. Students are often more motivated to learn when they are engaged in an activity that is enjoyable and fun. This can help students develop critical thinking and problem-solving skills that are important to understanding biological concepts.

Second, games can also provide a more immersive learning experience. They can simulate real-life situations and allow students to explore the consequences of their actions in a controlled environment. For example, a game that simulates the effects of climate change on a particular ecosystem can help students understand the complex interactions between environmental factors, species, and habitats.

Third, games can also provide immediate feedback to students. As they play the game, students receive feedback on their decisions and actions, allowing them to quickly assess the consequences of their choices. This can help students develop a deeper understanding of biological concepts by helping them see cause-and-effect relationships in action.

Finally, games can also be used to teach specific skills, such as data analysis or experimental design. By incorporating these skills into a game setting, students can develop an understanding of how these skills are used in real-life scientific research.

Overall, the importance of harnessing the power of games in enhancing student learning of biological concepts lies in their ability to provide an engaging, interactive, immersive, and feedback-rich learning environment. content:Speaker assistant says: Certainly! Here is a sample project-based intervention using games to improve your students' literature identification and evaluation skills in Biology:

Project Title: "Science Literature Scavenger Hunt"

Objective: The objective of this project is to help students develop their science literature identification and evaluation skills by having them search for scientific articles related to a particular biology concept and critically evaluate the articles based on predetermined criteria. Materials Needed: Computers or devices with internet access, access to scientific databases (such as PubMed or Google Scholar), a list of predetermined criteria for evaluating articles, and game-based evaluation worksheets. Steps:

1. Introduction: Begin by introducing the concept of science literature identification and evaluation to your students. Provide them with examples of different types of scientific articles (such as research papers, review articles, and case studies) and explain how the articles can be used to build scientific knowledge. 2. Scavenger Hunt: Divide students into groups and provide them with a biology concept they will be exploring. For example, the groups may be assigned to explore the concept of gene regulation in prokaryotes. Instruct each group to search for scientific articles related to the assigned concept using scientific databases. 3. Criteria Evaluation: Provide each group with a predetermined set of criteria for evaluating the scientific articles they have found. The criteria may include things such as the reliability of the source, the relevance of the research question to the concept explored, and the quality of the data presented. Have each group evaluate the articles against the criteria and present their findings to the class. 4. Game-Based Evaluation: Design game-based worksheets to reinforce the students' evaluation of science literature, and provide feedback on the factors they have considered to evaluate the articles' quality. 5. Reflection: After completing the scavenger hunt, have each student write a reflection on what they learned about science literature identification and evaluation. Ask them to discuss what they found challenging, what they found interesting, and how they might use the skills they have developed in the future. Assessment: Assess students' science literature identification and evaluation skills by evaluating the quality of the articles they have selected and the criteria they have used to evaluate them. Additionally, evaluate how well they were able to complete the game-based evaluation worksheet and reflection writing. By using games in this project-based intervention, you can help your students develop important science literature identification and evaluation skills while promoting critical thinking and collaborative learning. context:This project aims to enhance students’ ability to critically analyze scientific articles related to biology concepts through a game-based approach. content:Speaker user says: The Master's programme Molecular and Cellular Life Sciences (MCLS) takes a multidisciplinary approach to molecules, cells and organisms. The programme provides students with the expertise to optimally address major scientific challenges and societal issues, such as human diseases and sustainable growth, as well as for innovative research in (plant)biotech industry. The interplay of biomolecules in cells and organisms takes a central role in this programme.
Students will develop extensive knowledge and skills to be successful in many areas of the Life Sciences. The program is focused on cell signalling, membrane biogenesis and intracellular transport mechanisms, as well as the methods of biochemistry, cell biology, computational biology, proteomics and genomics. All of these can be needed to approach problems in the field.
Powerful modelling systems which have already been established will be even more effective when used in combination with biochemical knowledge and genome data. The programme offers expert training in several of the most prominent biological models, including bacteria, fungi, plants and animals, as well as cultured mammalian and insect cells.
In the past, research has often focused on a single level of observation: molecules, cells, tissues or organisms. Courses and projects in the programme emphasize crossing former boundaries. The current challenge is to bring all these levels together into a comprehensive understanding of life. This systems biology approach, calls for a broad set of competences which are all available at the Utrecht University.
This acquired knowledge can be used to work on solutions in the biomedical field but also in the field of plant biology, biotechnology (e.g. Industrial enzymes for biofuels) and nanotechnology (e.g. Nanoparticles in medicine).
Research groups from the departments of Biology, Chemistry, Pharmacy, Physics and faculties of Medicine and Veterinary Medicine are involved in this interdisciplinary programme. The MCLS programme is directly linked to the PhD-programmes of the Bijvoet Center for Biomolecular Research, the Institute for Biodynamics and Biocomplexity and the PhD programme of Computational Life Sciences.
Our programme is directly linked to the PhD programmes Biomembranes, Molecular Life Sciences and Computational Life Sciences of the Graduate School of Life Sciences. content:Speaker user says: I'm not sure if it is still the case, but there was a time when Kuhn's book was the most frequently cited book in scientific literature. With all respect to my fellow reviewers, it might be a tad bit arrogant to dismiss such a book as "puerile." Before Kuhn, we were taught in school that scientific progress was linear, that it was an unending progression of refinements and developments, with one "truth" leading to the next "truth." Kuhn's insights including pointing out that such a linear progression was mostly a lie. His thesis was that the major developments in science were mostly revolutionary. That some "truths" turned out to be False. Astronomy was revolutionized by Galileo and Copernicus, and man was divested from the center of the universe. Physics was revolutionized by Newton. Biology and Darwin. It didn't hurt that plate tectonics came along shortly after Kuhn published, and Kuhn looked like his model was predictive, too. Part of Kuhn's impact, I have to admit, was a result of the time which the book was first published. In the middle and late 1960s, questioning authority was the heart of any undergraduate's thinking, and Kuhn's ideas were read by some as a license to question all authority. Perhaps as a consequence, Kuhn's model has been carried by other writers beyond all reason, with everyone from sociologists to New Age fuzzies usurping his terminology, making "paradigm shift" a nearly instant cliche. But his influence has gone far beyond those who want to mis-apply his ideas to everything from post-modern dance to sociobiology. Uniformitarianism has been bloodied, perhaps permanently. By geologists, evolutionists, archaeologists and more; the influence has been pervasive and real. Stephen Jay Gould may or may not subscribe to "Structure," but he has sure demolished uniformitarianism in evolution. I disagree with those who regard "Structure" as "the most important" anything. But it unquestionably has been stunningly influential, and any serious student of science or philosophy, I believe, will be reading this book a hundred years from now. And apart from its influence and impact, the book still reads well almost 40 years on. It's fun and, if you enjoy seeing the world stood on its ear, you'll like Kuhn's approach. context:The author discusses the enduring impact of the book "The Structure of Scientific Revolutions" by Thomas Kuhn, highlighting its influence on various fields and the book’s continued relevance over time. keywords: Kuhn, paradigm shift, scientific progress, evolution, uniformity, plate tectonics, Stephen Jay Gould, structure, science, philosophy. tags: Science, Philosophy, History of Science, Paradigm Shifts, Evolution, Sociology, Archaeology

content:Speaker assistant says: The guitar pedal is an electronic device that modifies the sound of an electric guitar. It has been a significant tool in the development of rock music since the mid-20th century. In the 1950s, guitar pedals were bulky and required vacuum tubes, making them heavy and costly. However, in the 1960s, the introduction of solid-state technology pushed the development of smaller and more affordable guitar pedals.

One of the earliest and most influential guitar pedals was the fuzz pedal. This distortion effect created a gritty, distorted sound that became iconic in rock music. Bands like the Rolling Stones, Jimi Hendrix, and the Kinks used fuzz pedals in their music, helping to shape the sound of rock music in the 1960s.

Later, other types of pedals were developed, including phasers, chorus, reverb, and delay. These effects have been used by countless guitarists, including Eddie Van Halen, Eric Clapton, and Eddie Hazel, to create unique and experimental sounds that have become a staple in the genre.

The impact of guitar pedals on rock music is undeniable. They have expanded the range of sounds that a guitar can produce, allowing musicians to push boundaries and create new sonic landscapes. content:Speaker user says: The 27th Singapore International Film Festival (SGIFF) kicked off on 23rd November and we delve into the exploration of digital space.
Watching TV used to be a communal activity with the family, and movie theatres were exciting places to hang out with friends as we stuff our faces with popcorn, but now, technology gives us a push and we fall backwards into a couch at home, streaming movies and dramas online with a subscription fee of about $12 a month.
We find out from three SGIFF forum speakers, Missy Laney, Lionel Chok, and Scott Kaplan, via email interviews, on whether Virtual Reality can be a game changer, and how the Internet is a boon and a bane for filmmakers.
The challenge of the new-age behavioural phenomenon is not only finding the platforms to host your show, but also adopting various marketing strategies to promote it.
It boils down to the basics of marketing: Knowing what you really want to achieve.
Scott Kaplan, SVP in Global Sales at Gunpowder & Sky Distribution, points out that film distribution in digital space is a reaction to macro-shifts in human behaviour.
Co-produced by Leonardo DiCaprio, ‘Before The Flood’ was broadcasted on NatGeo as well as online platforms like Daily Motion.
To produce ‘For The Love Of Spock’, over USD$600,000 was crowd-funded on Kickstarter.
It’s easy to mistake online marketing as mindless updates, which can dilute your film’s branding.
Missy Laney, Film Strategist and formerly the Director of Creative Initiatives at BitTorrent, believes it has been easier than ever to reach your audience, but keeping their attention is tough.
A monthly subscription doesn’t really justify the money pumped into physical production. Film creators are losing money and are desperately trying to work the digital space towards their advantage.
“Additionally, fans can also interact with films now as funders and backers using crowd funding so that’s another big shift in the relationship we have with movies now,” says Missy Laney.
Virtual Reality As Our New Reality?
Lionel Chok is a Singapore filmmaker, director, and many other titles under his belt. From how he sees it, Lionel thinks the digital trend and VR technology are two great things amalgamated.
“This is something very powerful. We are currently developing apps for VR content to be published in an online store. As the cost of app development has reduced, this is definitely going to impact filmmakers, as the Play Store or the iOS store will now become a method of distribution. The platforms are also evolving and content can be priced across different stores for all demographics,” says Lionel.
While the local movie scene in Singapore is still quite dry, VR is a new direction for aspiring local filmmakers. Having a passion in Augmented and Virtual Reality, Lionel is excited about its future.
Future of Cinema Forum – Independent Film: Navigating the Digital Space, as part of the Singapore International Film Festival, will be held on 26 November 2016, 1pm at *SCAPE.

content:Speaker user says: What are the most common injuries in basketball and how are they treated? context:back injuries keywords: basketball, injuries, treatment, common tags: concussion, recovery, basketball

content:Speaker assistant says: 1. Ankle sprains: This is the most common injury in basketball. It occurs when the ankle twists, turns or rolls beyond its normal range of motion. Treatment includes R.I.C.E (rest, ice, compression and elevation), physical therapy, and ankle braces.

2. Knee injuries: Knee injuries commonly occur due to high-impact activities like jumping and landing, which puts a lot of strain on the knees. Common knee injuries in basketball include ACL, MCL, and meniscus tears, as well as patella tendonitis (jumper's knee). Treatment can involve physical therapy, rest, surgery, and rehabilitation.

3. Concussion: Concussions occur when there's a blow to the head or a sudden jolt that causes the brain to move back and forth in the skull. Players with a concussion should be immediately withdrawn from play and evaluated by a healthcare professional.

4. Back injuries: Basketball players may suffer from back pain or even herniated discs due to the repetitive jumping and twisting movements. Treatment includes physical therapy, rest, and surgery in severe cases.

5. Finger injuries: Finger injuries like sprains and fractures can result from injuries during ball handling, passing, or during collisions with other players. Treatment may include R.I.C.E, splinting or casting, and surgery in some cases.

Overall, prevention is key, players should maintain good physical condition, wear proper protective gear, and adhere to safety rules and proper techniques during play. context:concussion keywords: ankle sprains, knee injuries, concussion, back injuries, finger injuries tags: knee injuries, recovery, basketball
